abstract: Abstract Autism spectrum disorder is a complex neurodevelopmental disease characterized by altered cortical network excitability. Recent genetic studies have identified deep layer V cortical pyramidal neurons in the frontal cortex as central to autism pathophysiology, yet the cortical circuits, plasticity mechanisms and molecular signalling pathways involved remain poorly understood. Layer V pyramidal neurons consist of two main types with distinct functional roles: intratelencephalic neurons, which respond to low-frequency stimulation and project within the cortex and striatum, and pyramidal tract neurons, which are tuned to theta-frequency inputs and convey information to subcortical structures. Determining which of these two neuron types is more critical to autism pathophysiology and whether disruptions in their synaptic connectivity or intrinsic excitability contribute to autism-related dysfunctions would significantly advance our understanding of the disorder. Integrins, a family of cell adhesion molecules, are vital for neuronal function. The gene encoding β3 integrin ( ITGB3 ) is genetically linked to autism spectrum disorder, with rare mutations identified in affected individuals, while Itgb3 knockout mice exhibit autism-like behaviours, including impaired social memory and increased grooming. However, it remains unclear why loss of β3 integrin is associated with autism spectrum disorder, how it disrupts cortical circuits, and which plasticity mechanisms and molecular pathways are involved. Here, we demonstrate that β3 integrin selectively regulates the excitability of pyramidal tract neurons in the medial prefrontal cortex. Using electrophysiology, proteomics and molecular approaches, we show that β3 integrin regulates the gain, adaptation and precision of action potential discharge by controlling the surface expression of Ca 2+ -activated SK2 channels. Genetic ablation of Itgb3 impaired intrinsic excitability and SK2 channel function in pyramidal tract neurons, with no effects in intratelencephalic neurons. Furthermore, we identified Tau, a protein traditionally linked to neurodegenerative diseases, as part of the SK2 channel interactome. Proteomic analyses revealed altered protein kinase A-dependent phosphorylation of Tau in Itgb3 knockout mice, while protein kinase A inhibition restored SK2 channel currents, thereby connecting phosphorylation changes to excitability deficits. Our findings expand the current mechanistic framework linking signalling pathway dysfunctions to cortical excitability deficits, highlighting the dysregulation of pyramidal tract neuron excitability as a core feature of autism pathophysiology and demonstrating the involvement of β3 integrin, SK2 channels, Tau and PKA in this process. Because pyramidal tract neurons serve as final integrators of cortical computations before relaying information outside the cortex, their impaired excitability may disrupt communication with subcortical targets, contributing to the complex pathophysiology of autism spectrum disorder.

Experimental model
Itgb3

Whole-cell patch-clamp recordings were performed as previously described
16
and are reported in detail in the
Supplementary material
. Unsupervised cluster analysis was conducted using Igor Pro 9.02 and GraphPad Prism. We standardized the electrophysiological properties through
z
-scoring and used the Euclidean distance as the measure of dissimilarity.
Retrograde labelling
The coordinates (anterior-posterior/medial-lateral/dorsal-ventral from bregma) for the stereotaxic injections were −4.16/±0.40/−5.65 mm for the pontine nuclei and 1.98/± 0.40/−1.00 mm for the contralateral cortex.
Histology
To reconstruct the dendritic morphology, the intracellular solution was supplemented with 2 mg/ml of Neurobiotin (Vector Laboratories) and the slices processed as described in the
Supplementary material
.
Immunohistochemistry
As described in detail in the
Supplementary material
, we used the following primary antibodies for immunohistochemistry: rabbit anti-SK2 (1:200; Cat. No. SK2-Rb-Af500; Frontier Institute), rabbit monoclonal anti-β3 integrin (1:100; Cat. No. 13166, Cell Signaling), chicken anti-GFP antibody (1:1000; Cat. No.AB13970, Abcam) and rabbit anti-Er81 antibody (1:200; Cat. No. Ab81086, Abcam).
Western blotting
As described in detail in the
Supplementary material
, we used the following antibodies for western blotting: rabbit anti-β3 integrin (1:200; Cat. No. 4702, Cell Signaling), rabbit anti-SK2 (1:200; Cat. No. SK2-Rb-Af500, Frontier Institute), mouse anti-phospho Tau (AT8, Ser202/Thr205; 1:2000; Cat. No. MN1020, ThermoFisher), mouse anti-Tau (TAU-5; 1:1000; Cat. No. AHB0042, ThermoFisher) and rabbit anti-β-tubulin III (1:1000; Cat. No. T2200, Sigma).
Immunoprecipitation
As described in detail in the
Supplementary material
, we used the following antibodies for immunoprecipitation: hamster anti-β3 integrin (Cat. No. 553343; BD Pharmingen), rabbit anti-SK2 (Cat. No. SK2-Rb-Af500, Frontier Institute), hamster IgG (Cat. No. PA5-33219 ThermoFisher) and rabbit anti-RFP (Cat. No. 600-401-379, Rockland).
RNA extraction and RT-qPCR
Total RNA was extracted as previously described.
17
Data were normalized to GAPDH, β-actin (ACTB) and HPRT1 by the multiple internal control gene method with GeNorm algorithm.
18
Sequences of primers used are as in Jaudon
et al
.
10
Immuno-electron microscopy
Immunohistochemical reactions were performed using the pre-embedding immunogold method, as previously described
19
and detailed in the
Supplementary material
. Briefly, sections were incubated with an anti-SK2 antibody (Cat. No. Rb-Af500; amino acids 536–574 from mouse SK2; Frontier Institute; 3–5 μg/ml), followed by incubation with a goat anti-rabbit IgG coupled to 1.4 nm gold (Nanoprobes Inc.). The specificity of the anti-SK2 antibody was described previously.
20
,
21
Proteomics
Brain slices were divided into three experimental groups: (i) Sham: slices kept at 30°C for 30 min; (ii) Forskolin: slices treated with the adenylyl cyclase activator Forskolin (25 µM; Cat. No. 1099, Tocris) and the phosphodiesterase inhibitor Ro 20-1724 (50 µM; Cat. No. 0415, Tocris) for 15 min at 30°C; and (iii) cAMPS-Rp: slices treated with the PKA inhibitor cAMPS-Rp (100 µM; Cat. No. A165, Sigma) for 30 min at 30°C. Slices were then homogenized and prepared for proteomic analysis as previously described
22
and as reported in detail in the
Supplementary material
. All data-independent acquisition (DIA) raw files were processed using Spectronaut version 18
23
with a library-free approach (directDIA) under BGS Phospho PTM Workflow settings.
Statistical analysis
Statistical differences were assessed using one-way ANOVA followed by the Sidak post-test, two-way ANOVA test followed by the Sidak or Fisher least significant difference post-tests, three-way ANOVA followed by the Sidak post-test or analysis of covariance and chi-squared test, as indicated (GraphPad Prism 10). Average data are expressed as mean ± standard error of the mean.

body:
Introduction
A central goal of autism spectrum disorder (ASD) research is to understand how ASD risk genes shape brain information processing at the circuit, neuronal ensemble and single-neuron levels. Over the last decade, genetic studies have identified deep layer V cortical pyramidal neurons in the frontal cortex as crucial to ASD pathophysiology.
1
,
2
However, critical questions remain regarding which cortical circuits, plasticity mechanisms and molecular signalling pathways in this brain region are most relevant to ASD. These gaps present significant challenges in understanding how genetic susceptibility leads to cortical dysfunction.
Layer V pyramidal neurons are classified into two major types based on their connectivity and intrinsic excitability. The first type, intratelencephalic (IT) neurons, respond primarily to slow stimulation (<2 Hz) and project exclusively to the neocortex and striatum. The second type, pyramidal tract (PT) neurons, are tuned to theta-frequency stimulation (4–10 Hz) and project to the pons and spinal cord, with collateral projections to the ipsilateral cortex, striatum and thalamus.
3
Determining which of these two neuron types—IT or PT—plays a more prominent role in ASD pathophysiology, and whether defects in their connectivity or intrinsic excitability are primarily involved, would significantly advance our understanding of how information processing is disrupted in ASD.
Integrins are a diverse family of cell adhesion molecules (CAMs) that respond to mechanical and chemical cues to regulate various aspects of cellular behaviour. Initially recognized for their roles in neuronal migration and neurite outgrowth, neuronal integrins are now known to play essential roles in synaptic plasticity.
4-10
Notably, genetic studies have linked
ITGB3
, the gene encoding β3 integrin, to ASD across different population cohorts, with rare mutations being identified in individuals with ASD.
11-14
Furthermore,
Itgb3
knockout (KO) mice exhibit autism-like phenotypes, including impaired social memory and increased grooming.
15
However, it remains unclear why loss of β3 integrin is associated with ASD, whether it disrupts cortical circuits, and if so, which cellular and molecular mechanisms are involved.
Here, we identify β3 integrin as a key modulator of PT neuron excitability in the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC). Through a combination of electrophysiology, proteomics and molecular approaches, we demonstrate that β3 integrin regulates the gain, adaptation and precision of action potential (AP) discharge by controlling the surface expression of Ca
2+
-activated SK2 channels. Genetic ablation of
Itgb3
impaired intrinsic excitability and SK2 channel function in PT neurons, but not IT neurons. Moreover, we identified Tau, a protein traditionally associated with neurodegenerative diseases, as part of the SK2 channel interactome. Proteomic analyses revealed altered protein kinase A (PKA)-dependent phosphorylation of Tau in
Itgb3
KO mice, while PKA inhibition restored SK2 channel currents, thereby linking phosphorylation changes to excitability deficits.
Our findings expand the current mechanistic framework linking signalling pathway dysfunctions to excitability deficits in cortical PT neurons, demonstrating the involvement of β3 integrin, SK2 channels, Tau and PKA in this process. Because PT neurons serve as final integrators of cortical computations before relaying information outside the cortex, defects in their excitability may disrupt overall cortical output, thus contributing to the complex pathophysiology of ASD.

Results
β3 integrin is enriched in layer V pyramidal neurons of the medial prefrontal cortex
To determine the role of β3 integrin in the brain, we first examined whether it was enriched in a specific brain region. Western blot analysis of the cortex and hippocampus from wild-type (WT),
Itgb3
+/−
(Het) and
Itgb3
−/−
(KO) mice at postnatal Day 14 (P14) and P60 revealed higher levels of β3 integrin in the cortex compared to the hippocampus at both developmental stages (
Fig. 1A
and
B
). We next used immunohistochemistry to assess the localization of β3 integrin in the mPFC. β3 integrin was enriched in deep cortical layers, particularly in layer V (
Fig. 1C
and
D
), suggesting a circuit specific role for this CAM. The absence of fluorescence in
Itgb3
KO mice sections (
Fig. 1C
and
D
), along with supporting transcriptomic data from both mouse and human studies,
1
,
24
,
25
confirmed the validity of this finding.

Since α3β1 integrin regulates dendritic arborization of CA1 hippocampal pyramidal neurons,
26
,
27
we conducted Sholl analysis on neurobiotin-filled layer V pyramidal neurons of the mPFC. PT neurons were identified by their thick apical dendritic tufts, and IT neurons by their thin apical dendritic tufts (with the discriminant threshold set at 50 apical tuft intersections). We found no significant differences in dendritic arborization between WT and
Itgb3
KO mice for either PT or IT neurons (
Fig. 1E
and
F
and
Supplementary Fig. 1C
). Likewise, there were no differences in cortical layer thickness between genotypes (
Supplementary Fig. 1A
and
B
).
We concluded that loss of β3 integrin does not result in overt morphological changes in the mPFC.
Cell-type-specific electrophysiological properties of layer V pyramidal neurons in WT and
Itgb3
KO mice
We next examined whether β3 integrin regulates the functional properties of mPFC layer V pyramidal neurons. To identify neuron types based on electrophysiological properties, we patched a total of 55 WT and 46
Itgb3
KO neurons and performed unsupervised hierarchical cluster analysis on a set of 14 electrophysiological parameters, encompassing subthreshold (resonance frequency, resonance strength, input resistance, membrane capacitance, resting membrane potential) and AP properties [rheobase, voltage threshold, amplitude, maximal slope of the depolarization phase, maximal negative slope of the repolarization phase, half-width, afterhyperpolarization (AHP) amplitude]. In both genotypes, unsupervised clustering identified two major classes of pyramidal neurons (
Fig. 2A
), with properties consistent with those previously described for PT and IT neurons in the rat mPFC.
28
To visualize the collective differences in the properties of these physiologically defined neuron types, we used principal component analysis (PCA) for dimensionality reduction. In PCA, the distance between neurons represents differences in physiological properties, making neurons with similar properties cluster together (
Fig. 2B
and
Supplementary Fig. 2A
and
B
). To confirm the validity of our classification, we used a retrograde virus expressing EGFP (rAAV2-retro)
29
injected into the ipsilateral pons or contralateral mPFC, to label PT neurons projecting to the pons (cortico-pontine PT neurons) or IT neurons projecting to the contralateral mPFC (commissural IT neurons), respectively (
Fig. 6A
). Unsupervised hierarchical clustering neatly segregated the retrogradely labelled neurons into PT and IT types based on the injection site (green and red stars in
Fig. 2A
; green and red circled plus symbols in
Fig. 2B
).

To determine if β3 integrin influences resonance properties, we injected a sinusoidal current with constant amplitude that increased linearly in frequency from 0 to 15 Hz (chirp stimulus;
Fig. 2C
). Analysis of the impedance amplitude in response to the chirp stimulus revealed that the higher resonance frequency and resonance strength characteristic of PT neurons compared to IT neurons were maintained in
Itgb3
KO mice (
Fig. 2C–E
and
Supplementary Fig. 2C
, left).
Consistent with these findings, PT neurons exhibited also greater voltage sag and rebound depolarization in response to hyperpolarizing current steps in both genotypes (
Supplementary Fig. 2D
). Furthermore, PT neurons had lower input resistance and a more depolarized membrane potential than IT neurons irrespective of the genotype (
Supplementary Fig. 2E
). Indeed, resonance frequency, input resistance and membrane potential were sufficient to effectively distinguish between PT and IT neuron types in both WT and
Itgb3
KO mice (
Supplementary Fig. 2F
).
PT and IT neurons also exhibit several differences in supra-threshold membrane properties.
28
,
30
We therefore analysed the first AP at rheobase. In line with previous findings,
28
APs in WT PT neurons exhibited higher rheobase, lower voltage threshold, larger amplitude, faster rise and decay slopes, and shorter duration (
Fig. 2F
and
G
and
Supplementary Fig. 2G
). Similar to the subthreshold properties, the AP characteristics of PT and IT neurons in
Itgb3
KO mice were indistinguishable from those of the respective WT neuron types (
Fig. 2F
and
G
and
Supplementary Fig. 2G
).
In the somatosensory cortex, the AHP following a single AP is larger in PT neurons compared to IT neurons.
30
In the mPFC, we observed a similar pattern in WT neurons (
Fig. 2H
and
I
). Surprisingly, however, the AHP of PT neurons was significantly reduced in
Itgb3
KO mice compared to WT mice, while IT neurons showed no significant AHP difference between genotypes (
Fig. 2H
and
I
).
In summary, a broad-spectrum, unbiased analysis of the electrophysiological properties of mPFC layer V pyramidal neurons indicates a specific role for β3 integrin in regulating the AHP size in PT neurons.
β3 integrin regulates the apamin-sensitive mAHP current in pyramidal tract neurons
In cortical pyramidal neurons, a large proportion of the AHP and its underlying currents are mediated by Ca
2+
-activated, apamin-sensitive SK channels.
30-34
We therefore investigated whether SK channels differentially contribute to the AHP in mPFC layer V pyramidal neurons. In all conditions, the SK channel-specific blocker apamin reduced the AHP, but the reduction was significantly larger in WT PT neurons compared to the other three conditions (
Supplementary Fig. 3A
and
B
). This suggests that SK channels are more robustly activated in WT PT neurons than in WT IT neurons following a single AP, and points to a specific role for β3 integrin in regulating the SK channel-dependent AHP in PT neurons.
Given these differences, we next characterized the underlying SK channel-mediated medium AHP current (mI
AHP
). To record the mI
AHP
in mPFC layer V pyramidal neurons, we used a protocol effective in isolating this current in various neuron types.
31
,
35
,
36
We depolarized the membrane from a holding potential of −50 mV to a range of potentials (−40 to +100 mV) for 100 ms, in the presence of the Na
+
channel blocker TTX and the K
+
channel blocker TEA, to induce Ca
2+
influx through voltage-gated Ca
2+
channels (VGCCs). Upon returning the membrane potential to −50 mV, we isolated a tail current closely resembling the mI
AHP
recorded in other neuron types (
Fig. 3
and
Supplementary Fig. 3C
). The mI
AHP
was entirely apamin-sensitive up to a depolarizing step of +40 mV (
Fig. 3A
and
Supplementary Fig. 3C
), with half-maximal activation voltages of 13.1 ± 3.2 mV, −0.7 ± 3.8 mV, −6.6 ± 2.0 mV and −8.4 ± 2.9 mV for WT PT, KO PT, WT IT and KO IT neurons, respectively (
Supplementary Fig. 3D
). Thus, we used a depolarizing step to +40 mV in all subsequent experiments.

Cell-type-specific regulation of layer V pyramidal neuron firing by β3 integrin
The Ca
2+
-activated mI
AHP
and its underlying SK channels are integral components of a feedback loop that regulates AP firing.

,
38

Fig. 4A–C
). The second protocol, aimed at assessing the regularity of spike discharge, used 10-s depolarizing currents (
Fig. 4D
and
E
). With both protocols, we detected no significant differences in the gain of AP discharge between genotypes for IT neurons (
Fig. 4
).

β3 integrin and SK channels regulate spike frequency adaptation in layer V pyramidal neurons in a cell-type specific manner
In proximal apical dendrites of pyramidal neurons, intracellular Ca
2+
typically peaks at around 300 nM following a single AP and increases during sustained trains of APs (≥10 Hz), reaching a steady-state value within the first 3–4 APs.
40
,
41
Afterwards, Ca
2+
levels fluctuate around a plateau that scales linearly with AP frequency.
40
Since SK channels are activated by Ca
2+
concentrations similar to those induced by APs (EC
50
≈ 300 nM),
42
,
43
they are well-positioned to provide negative feedback regulating early spike frequency adaptation and the time fidelity of AP discharge. Early spike frequency adaptation refers to the reduction in AP firing rate during the initial few hundred milliseconds of a stimulus of constant intensity.
37
To quantify spike frequency adaptation, we plotted the relative difference between the instantaneous firing frequency (F
x
in
Fig. 5B
and
C
and
Supplementary Fig. 5B
and
C
) and the steady-state firing frequency (F
ss
in
Fig. 5B
and
C
and
Supplementary Fig. 5B
and
C
), an index ranging from −1 (indicating maximum spike frequency acceleration) to +1 (indicating maximum spike frequency adaptation). To facilitate comparisons across cell types, genotypes and pharmacological manipulations, we measured this index for the minimum current injection required to elicit at least 12 APs in 1 s. This ensures sustained firing without causing fatigue under all experimental conditions (
Fig. 4
and
Supplementary Fig. 4
). Apamin significantly affected spike frequency adaptation only in WT PT neurons. It increased the adaptation index for the first AP from 0.21 ± 0.06 to 0.40 ± 0.06 and the average adaptation index for APs 3–6 from 0.04 ± 0.03 to 0.10 ± 0.03. It also reduced the early adaptation time constant (measured in AP numbers) from 0.80 ± 0.16 to 0.21 ± 0.10 (
Fig. 5A
and
B
, top). These findings are counterintuitive, as SK channels are generally thought to promote early adaptation due to their progressive activation from increasing Ca
2+
entry during initial APs. However, if the Ca
2+
entry following the first AP is sufficient to strongly activate SK channels, with little further activation from subsequent APs, SK channels may actually limit early spike frequency adaptation.
44
Similar effects, where SK channel blockade enhances early adaptation, have also been observed in motoneurons and PT neurons of the somatosensory cortex.

β3 integrin is required for precision of action potential discharge in pyramidal tract neurons
A primary function of cortical neurons is to convert inputs into reliable outputs. Thus, in addition to spike frequency adaptation, the precision of AP discharge is a key temporal parameter for neuronal coding.
47
We quantified the regularity of AP timing using the Fano factor of the AP count at various bin widths (
Fig. 5F
and
Supplementary Fig. 5F
), with smaller Fano factor values indicating more regular firing patterns.
48
To enable comparisons across conditions, we calculated the Fano factor for current injections that elicited APs at an average rate of 10 Hz, which is typical for up states of layer V pyramidal neurons.
49
,
50
WT PT neurons exhibited a more regular firing pattern than
Itgb3
KO PT neurons. Moreover, apamin increased the Fano Factor only in WT PT neurons, thereby reducing the differences in AP regularity between genotypes (
Fig. 5D–F
). In contrast, apamin slightly but significantly increased the Fano Factor in both WT and
Itgb3
KO IT neurons (
Supplementary Fig. 5D–F
).
In summary, these findings suggest that the mI
AHP
contributes to the regularity of AP discharge in both PT and IT neurons, but this regulatory mechanism is selectively disrupted in PT neurons of
Itgb3
KO mice.
Differential expression of SK2 channels between pyramidal tract and intratelencephalic neurons
Our data thus far reveal an unexpected and specific role of β3 integrin in regulating the saturation, adaptation and precision of AP discharge in PT neurons via the mI
AHP
. Since alterations in intrinsic excitability, whether physiological or pathological, can profoundly impact the computational properties of the mPFC,
51-57
our next goal was to uncover the molecular mechanisms underlying this regulation.
To this end, we first examined whether SK2 channels were differentially expressed in layer V pyramidal neurons across neuron types and genotypes. Among the two apamin-sensitive SK channels (SK2 and SK3),
58
,
59
only SK2 is expressed in layer V pyramidal neurons,
60
,
61
specifically its short, non-synaptic isoform.
62-64
We therefore focused on SK2 channels. To distinguish between PT and IT neurons, we injected an EGFP-expressing retrograde virus (rAAV2-retro)
29

Fig. 6A
). Remarkably, corticopontine PT neurons expressed higher levels of SK2 channels compared to commissural IT neurons (
Fig. 6B
and
C
). This aligns with our electrophysiological data, showing a larger mI
AHP
in WT PT neurons compared to WT IT neurons (
Fig. 3
), as well as with recent single-cell sequencing data from mice and humans.

We next investigated whether differences in functional coupling between VGCCs and SK channels could account for some of the observed variations in mI

and

Itgb3
KO prefrontal cortex, Tau phosphorylation at Ser202 was higher under basal conditions, strongly elevated by Forskolin and decreased by cAMPS-Rp (
Fig. 8A
and
Supplementary Fig. 8
).

Discussion
Our findings reveal that the
Itgb3
KO mouse model of ASD exhibits dysregulation of intrinsic excitability in mPFC PT neurons, and demonstrate the involvement of SK2 channels, Tau and PKA in this process. First, by combining IHC and retrograde labelling, we show that β3 integrin is specifically enriched in layer V pyramidal neurons (
Figs 1
and
6
). Second, an unbiased screening of electrophysiological properties revealed that
Itgb3
KO mice exhibit a selective reduction in the AHP and underlying mI
AHP
in PT neurons, but not in IT neurons (
Figs 2
and
3
). Third, we identify significant deficits in the saturation, adaptation and precision of AP discharge in PT neurons of
Itgb3
KO mice (
Figs 4
and
5
). Fourth, using pharmacology and immuno-EM, we demonstrate that these excitability defects likely result from the intracellular trapping of SK2 channels in the absence of β3 integrin (
Fig. 7
and
Supplementary Fig. 7
). Finally, proteomic analysis revealed altered PKA-dependent phosphorylation of Tau at Ser202 in the SK2 channel interactome from the prefrontal cortex of
Itgb3
KO mice. Conversely, PKA inhibition restored SK2 channel-dependent currents in
Itgb3
KO PT neurons (
Fig. 8
), thereby establishing a mechanistic link between altered PKA-dependent phosphorylation and excitability defects associated with SK2 channels.
Over the past decade, genetic studies have implicated dysfunction in layer V cortical circuits of the frontal cortex as a major contributor to ASD risk.
1
,
2
Our findings indicate that a substantial part of this dysfunction may arise from impairments in the excitability of PT neurons, the primary output neurons of the cortex. Notably, mouse models of fragile X syndrome, a leading monogenic cause of ASD, also exhibit selective impairments in PT neuron excitability, involving the downregulation of HCN and BK channels, along with the upregulation of A-type K
+
channels.
75
,
76
IT and PT neurons perform distinct computational functions in the mPFC. IT neurons integrate multiple long-range inputs, mainly from other cortical areas, the thalamus, amygdala, ventral hippocampus and claustrum, while they project locally to PT neurons and, over long distances, only to other cortical areas and the striatum across both hemispheres.
77
They primarily act as temporal integrators, summing multiple sequential inputs to reinforce ongoing cortical computations.
78
By contrast, PT neurons receive abundant local inputs from IT neurons, along with some direct long-range inputs, mainly from other cortical areas and the thalamus, while providing minimal local output and instead projecting extensively to subcortical targets, including the ipsilateral striatum, thalamus, pons and various neuromodulatory centres.
77
PT neurons serve primarily as coincidence detectors, responding effectively to simultaneous inputs from multiple sources and broadcasting this information to subcortical regions.
78
The higher tonic firing rate of PT neurons compared to IT neurons enables them to respond efficiently to frequent synaptic inputs, a key feature for reliable subcortical information transfer.
28
Here, we show that one mechanism supporting this heightened excitability in PT neurons is the elevated expression of SK2 channels, which enables sustained high-frequency firing with minimal adaptation, ensuring a linear response to increasing input currents.
38
,
39
,
79
In
Itgb3
KO PT neurons, reduced SK2 channel levels enhance spike frequency adaptation and cause the relationship between injected current and AP number to plateau, resembling the response observed in IT neurons (
Figs 4
and
5A–C
and
Supplementary Fig. 5A–C
). Consequently, impairment of β3 integrin reduces the differences between PT and IT neurons in terms of AP gain and adaptation. It is plausible that enhanced spike frequency adaptation in PT neurons contributes to more stable internal activity states of cortical networks in ASD, a hypothesis supported by recent computational studies.
80
A third major consequence of reduced SK2 channel levels in
Itgb3
KO PT neurons is decreased AP precision (
Fig. 5D–F
), a phenomenon also observed in Purkinje cells and dopaminergic midbrain neurons.
35
,
81
Impaired AP precision may hinder the ability of PT neurons to function as coincidence detectors, which depends on the precise timing of APs in response to synaptic inputs.
47
,
78
This reduction in precision could disrupt the integration of cortical computations with simultaneous thalamic inputs in the mPFC, potentially compromising executive functions like decision-making, planning, problem-solving and social behaviour.
15
While SK2 channels are predominantly expressed in PT neurons, β3 integrin is expressed in both PT and IT neurons (
Fig. 6
). The differential impact of β3 integrin loss on these neuronal populations may arise because SK2-mediated currents and their effects on AP firing are already minimal in IT neurons, limiting the observable consequences of β3 integrin loss. In contrast, the higher expression and functional relevance of SK2 channels in PT neurons make them more susceptible to β3 integrin perturbations, resulting in a more pronounced disruption of SK2-mediated currents and AP regulation.
Previous research has shown that β3 integrin interactions with the extracellular matrix promote the elongation of thin dendritic spines in PT neurons and the synaptic localization of glutamate receptors, particularly in the context of homeostatic synaptic plasticity.
6-10
,
82-84
Loss-of-function mutations in β3 integrin identified in ASD patients
11-14
are therefore expected to impair synaptic connectivity, by reducing excitatory synaptic currents and the ability to form new synapses, as well as intrinsic excitability, by reducing SK2 channel expression, of PT neurons. While, at first approximation, these two effects could compensate for each other and help stabilize overall neuronal output, theoretical models predict that such neurons are likely to become more easily activated by otherwise irrelevant synaptic stimuli.
4
,
53
,
54
,
85
Unexpectedly, we find that β3 integrin, SK2 channels and Tau are components of the same multi-molecular signalling complex (
Figs 7C
and
8A–C
). Tau, a microtubule-associated protein, has traditionally been linked to neurodegenerative disorders, including Alzheimer’s disease and frontotemporal dementia.
86
However, emerging evidence suggests a potential role for Tau in ASD pathogenesis. Specifically, elevated serum levels of Tau have been reported in ASD patients,
87
and reducing Tau levels has been shown to alleviate autism-like symptoms in some ASD mouse models.
88
,
89
The involvement of Tau in ASD is thought to arise from its interaction with the ASD-related gene
PTEN
(phosphatase and tensin homolog), through which it inhibits PTEN activity.
88
While Tau hyperphosphorylation is typically linked to neurodegenerative conditions,
86
phosphorylation at Ser202 and Thr205, identified here as altered in
Itgb3
KO mice under both basal conditions and following PKA inhibition (
Fig. 8A–C
), is not induced by amyloid-β but rather by pharmacological treatments that promote network activity and Ca
2+
influx.
72
,
74
Phosphorylation at these sites leads Tau to translocate from dendritic spines to dendritic shafts, reducing glutamate receptor-dependent excitability.
73
,
74

At a more fundamental level, our findings indicate that alterations in cortical excitability following loss of β3 integrin are driven by changes in PKA-dependent signalling pathways that regulate SK2 channels. This novel pathway provides insight into the underlying causes of cortical dysfunction in ASD and highlights new potential therapeutic targets.
